newsitem.title: USA: Judge denies Ahmanson's move to delay Great Western vote.
newsitem.headline: Judge denies Ahmanson's move to delay Great Western vote.

text.p: In a blow to hostile suitor H.F. Ahmanson & Co., a judge ruled Tuesday that Great Western Financial Corp. shareholders may vote on a proposed $6.7 billion merger with white knight Washington Mutual Inc. on June 13.
The ruling leaves Ahmanson few options but to raise its bid, which would dilute its stock and leave the banking company open to criticism from its own stockholders.

The 41-page ruling by Chancellor Jack Jacobs in Delaware Chancery Court denied a motion by Ahmanson, the Irwindale, Calif.-based parent of Home Savings of America, that the merger vote be delayed for at least six weeks.

Ahmanson has fought since February to win the deal despite Great Western's rejection and a merger agreement, announced March 6, with Seattle-based Washington Mutual Inc., which would create the largest U.S. thrift with $86 billion in assets.

Chatsworth, Calif.-based Great Western said Tuesday it was pleased with the ruling. "Clearly, Ahmanson has its own interests in mind and not the best interests of Great Western stockholders," it said in a statement.
And, investment bankers working near Great Western, which has been a target of Ahmanson's overtures since February, expect more fireworks.

"None of Ahmanson's legal or regulatory challenges have worked. A bump (in the bid) is about the only thing left and I think they'll try anything," said one investment banker close to Chatsworth, Calif.-based Great Western.

Ahmanson is trying to get three people backing its bid elected to Great Western's board on June 13 and wanted to delay the vote on the Washington Mutual transaction so the new members have time to sway Great Western's board.
A spokeswoman for Ahmanson Tuesday said the company was studying the implications of the ruling and declined comment on whether or not it would raise its bid.
"We will be evaluating the situation," said another source close to Ahmanson and involved in the deal.
The board has already approved Washington Mutual's offer of 0.9 shares for each Great Western share and voted down Ahmanson's offer of 1.2 shares for each Great Western share.

"We are pleased to report that our timetable for completion remains on track. We still anticipate that the merger could be completed as soon as late June or early July, following the receipt of necessary shareholder and regulatory approvals," Washington Mutual said in a release.
Based on Tuesday's prices, Ahmanson's bid was valued at $48.30 a share, or about $6.73 billion, while Washington Mutual's bid was worth $48.38 a share, or about $6.74 billion.

In Jacobs' decision, he said "the result of an injunction would be the delay the ability of Washington Mutual, Great Western and their shareholders to begin realising the economic benefits expected to result from the merger.

"Delaying the merger would also significantly increase the risk that the value of Great Western would diminish, through losses of customers and key employees as a result of continued uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the bidding contest for control," he continued.
Sources near the thrifts and analysts said that Ahmanson faces a problem if it raises its bid because that could wind up diluting its stock.

"If Ahmanson sweetens their proposal meaningfully, there could be an investor backlash. They have to make sure the economics make sense or they could wind up hurting their chances," Campbell Chaney, analyst with Sandler O'Neill.
Another source close to the company cited these concerns. "There's no reason to believe that any bid we put on the table would get a different reaction," the source said.

Analysts said investors are favouring Seattle-based Washington Mutual's bid because it is a friendly transaction endorsed by Great Western's board and because of Washington Mutual Chairman Kerry Killinger's reputation and success in executing acquisitions, a total of 22 in the last 10 years.
In a recent interview, Killinger said he was confident Washington Mutual would proceed with the merger even if Ahmanson tries to raise its bid.
But one investment banker suggested that Ahmanson may wait until the last minute.

"A bump at the last minute could make Great Western's lives miserable. It could make it difficult to endorse the Washington Mutual deal, if Ahmanson raises the bid the night before the meeting and the value is higher," the banker said.
"If Ahmanson moves its exchange from 1.2 shares to 1.3 shares too far in advance, the market would punish the stock," the banker said.
